title: API Consistency and Error Quality
learning_outcomes: Explain how api consistency and error quality affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from shared error conventions to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on api consistency and error quality in validation, error handling, and api consistency. You will connect shared error conventions to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: API Consistency and Error Quality matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying shared error conventions deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 91 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 91: Shared error conventions → Consistent status codes → Correlation and support identifiers → Error response contract testing.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Validation errors, business conflicts, authentication failures, and unexpected server failures should be distinguishable and consistently represented. In this lesson, treat “API Consistency and Error Quality” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: Validate shape and business rules separately

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: API Consistency and Error Quality
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.test/problems/validation",
  "title": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid.",
  "errors": [{"field":"title","code":"required"}]
}
content_blocks.expected_output: The response uses an explicit, machine-readable validation error. The service should not include stack traces or secrets.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Shared error conventions”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Consistent status codes” and “Error response contract testing”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Distinguish client mistakes, business conflicts, and unexpected server failures. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating api consistency and error quality. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Shared error conventions” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for API Consistency and Error Quality with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating api consistency and error quality as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Validation errors, business conflicts, authentication failures, and unexpected server failures should be distinguishable and consistently represented. In this lesson, treat “API Consistency and Error Quality” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 92: Understanding an API Server.
